What Is Account-Based Marketing? A Small-Team Version

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 27 May 2026 · 7-minute read · Revenue

Account-based marketing (ABM) is a way of concentrating sales and marketing effort on a named set of companies that fit the product, rather than trying to reach everyone and hoping the right buyers respond. It fits sales of meaningful value that take time and involve several people; Forrester finds an average of 13 people involved in a B2B purchase. A small team can run it without a large platform: a short list, research on each account, one owner per account and measures that track account progress, not email volume.

A small B2B company does not always need thousands of leads. If ten customers could meaningfully change its revenue, it may make more sense to identify those customers and work deliberately to earn their business. That is account-based marketing.

What account-based marketing actually means

Start with a shortlist of companies whose problems the product can solve. Learn who is involved in the buying decision, why the timing may be right and what would make the company willing to talk. Use that knowledge to make outreach, content and follow-up relevant.

LinkedIn's marketing glossary defines ABM as "a strategic approach that focuses on targeting and engaging specific high-value accounts or companies" and describes three stages: account research, content creation for each account, and execution and measurement. A small team can do those jobs with ordinary research tools and a CRM rather than an enterprise software package.

This is not a mass-email sequence with someone's first name inserted. It is a coordinated way of deciding where limited sales and marketing effort should go. The unit of attention changes from the lead (one person who filled in a form) to the account (the company and the group of people inside it who will decide). Our comparison of lead scoring and account scoring covers what that change does to qualification.

When ABM is the right motion

ABM is a natural fit when a sale has meaningful value, takes time and involves several stakeholders. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. When that many people decide, reaching one of them through a form fill is not enough. Our explainer on the buying committee sets out the roles.

SignalABM likely fitsBroad inbound or product-led likely fits
Deal valueHigh enough that one win changes the quarterLow; volume carries the economics
Buyer identityYou can name target companies in advanceBuyers are anonymous until they arrive
Buying groupSeveral departments, technical and commercial diligenceOne person can buy alone
Sales cycleMonths, with stages that can stallDays, often self-serve
Example contextsFintech infrastructure sold to banks; AI for a regulated workflow; services for funds and custodiansLow-cost software, consumer apps

It is less suitable when the product is cheap, self-serve and bought spontaneously. The key question is whether knowing and contacting a particular company is worth the work involved.

What the evidence says, and what it does not

Most ABM research comes from people who practise it, so read it as direction rather than proof. Momentum ITSMA's benchmark study, run with the ABM Leadership Alliance and published in March 2023, surveyed 279 ABM heads and practitioners. It found 72% said ABM delivers higher ROI than other types of marketing, and ABM accounted for 28% of their 2022 marketing budgets. It also found only 17% of programmes were fully embedded in go-to-market strategy. Most programmes, in other words, are still bolted on.

Forrester's 2022 State of ABM survey found the most common reason for adopting account-based strategies was sourcing new pipeline, and Forrester advised against over-relying on sourcing metrics. It also found average ABM budgets of $590,000 excluding headcount, a figure far above what a small team will spend, and that 39% of programmes were still pilots.

The fair reading: ABM works for the people who choose it and run it well, which is a self-selected group. It is not automatically cheaper than other channels. It works when the value of winning a fitting account justifies the research and follow-up time.

A hundred opens are not a substitute for one serious buyer conversation.

Build a short list you can actually work

For a hypothetical fintech infrastructure company, a sensible starting list might be 20 to 50 accounts, not an arbitrarily large database. The right size depends on deal value and team capacity: a list is the right length when every account on it gets real research and a named owner.

For each account, record four things:

FieldWhat goes in itTest
FitWhy the product demonstrably solves this company's problemWould it pass your ideal customer profile?
Reason to talkA relevant, verified change: a launch, a hire, an expansion, a public statement, an introductionCan you link to the evidence?
Buying rolesLikely sponsor, evaluator, finance, security, legalDo you know at least two names?
Next stepOne person, one credible message, one follow-up ownerIs the owner written down?

Verify the signal rather than inventing a problem from a job title. A company launching a new payment product, hiring for treasury operations or expanding internationally may have a specific need. Our piece on signal-based outbound covers how to score those signals.

Run a small programme before buying a platform

Prepare a short research note for each account. Write a message based on the business problem, not biographical trivia. Support it with material that does a job for that reader: a relevant product explanation, technical documentation or a properly evidenced case study.

Use partner introductions, thoughtful email and professional communities where relevant. A small roundtable can help with conversations that need several stakeholders in the room. Coordinate follow-ups in a shared CRM, and give each account one owner so marketing and sales are not contacting the same people with conflicting messages.

Review the list every two weeks. Ask which accounts have progressed, what objections came up and whether the list still makes sense. Accounts that have shown no movement in two review cycles should be replaced, not chased harder. For the largest accounts, account planning for the top twenty describes the next level of depth.

Measure progress by account

Track what moves an account towards a decision:

  1. Relevant meetings. Conversations with people who hold part of the decision.
  2. Stakeholders engaged. How many of the buying roles you now know and have spoken to.
  3. Diligence completed. Technical, security or commercial review started or passed.
  4. Qualified opportunities and wins. The outcome, with the time from first contact recorded.

Include the team's research and follow-up hours in the economics. ABM is often more expensive per account than broad channels, and that is fine when the accounts are worth it.

lowob takeaways

  • Start with identifiable, high-fit buyers. A short, worked list beats a large, unworked one.
  • Research the business need. Personalise the reason to talk, not the greeting.
  • One owner per account. Coordinated sales and marketing, one coherent approach.
  • Read the ROI surveys carefully. They are self-reported by practitioners; measure your own account movement.

Common questions

What is account-based marketing in simple terms?

It is focusing sales and marketing effort on a named list of companies that fit the product, researching each one and coordinating outreach to the people who will make the decision, instead of generating as many leads as possible.

Is account-based marketing worth it for a small company?

It can be, when deals are valuable, buyers can be identified in advance and purchases involve several people. A small team can run it with 20 to 50 accounts, a CRM and disciplined research. It rarely pays for cheap, self-serve products.

How many accounts should an ABM programme target?

As many as the team can research properly and assign an owner to. For a small team that is often 20 to 50. The constraint is research and follow-up time, not the size of the database.

How do you measure account-based marketing?

By account progress: meetings with decision makers, buying roles engaged, diligence completed, qualified opportunities and wins. Email opens and clicks say little about whether an account is moving.
